subject: Social Science
title: The Village Well: Why Public Facilities Matter
hook: Why do all people in a city need access to water, schools, and hospitals?

slides.title: Public Facilities
slides.inSimpleWords: Services and resources that the government provides for all people to use.

slides.title: A Town Without Water
slides.storyContext: Priya's neighborhood has no public water supply. She walks 2 km daily to fetch water. Roshan cannot go to school because he must help carry water. Ajay, a municipal worker, realizes the town needs a public water project to serve everyone equally.
slides.inSimpleWords: Without public facilities, people—especially the poor—suffer.

image.alt: A Town Without Water — Public Facilities

slides.title: What Are Public Facilities?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Facilities provided by the government for all citizens to access freely or at low cost.

points.label: Aim
points.text: To ensure every person, rich or poor, can meet basic needs.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Water supply, electricity, schools, hospitals, roads, buses, parks.

example.problem: Priya cannot afford to buy water from a private seller. How does a public water supply help?
example.solution: Public water is provided by the government at low or no cost, so even poor families can access it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Public facilities are government services available to all people.

image.alt: What Are Public Facilities? — Public Facilities

slides.title: Types of Public Facilities

points.label: Health
points.text: Hospitals, clinics, immunization programs, maternal health services.

points.label: Education
points.text: Public schools, libraries, skill centers.

points.label: Water and Sanitation
points.text: Drinking water, sewage, toilets, waste management.

points.label: Transport
points.text: Buses, trains, roads, traffic lights.

points.label: Recreation
points.text: Parks, playgrounds, community centers.

example.problem: When Roshan gets sick, where should his family take him without paying too much?
example.solution: To a public hospital or government clinic, which charges little or nothing.

slides.inSimpleWords: Public facilities cover health, education, water, transport, and recreation.

image.alt: Types of Public Facilities — Public Facilities

slides.title: Why Public Facilities Are Important

points.label: Equality
points.text: Everyone gets the same basic services, regardless of income.

points.label: Health
points.text: Vaccinations and public clinics prevent disease in entire communities.

points.label: Education
points.text: Public schools allow poor children to learn and break the poverty cycle.

points.label: Economy
points.text: Good roads, electricity, and water help businesses and jobs grow.

points.label: Social Cohesion
points.text: Public spaces bring people together and build community.

example.problem: Why is public education important, not just private schools?
example.solution: Poor children cannot afford private school fees. Public schools ensure all children get education, creating a fair society.

slides.inSimpleWords: Public facilities ensure basic needs are met for all people, not just the rich.

image.alt: Why Public Facilities Are Important — Public Facilities

slides.title: Challenges in Providing Public Facilities

points.label: Funding
points.text: Government has limited money; priorities like defense compete with public services.

points.label: Growth
points.text: Growing population and cities make it hard to provide for all.

points.label: Maintenance
points.text: Facilities decay without upkeep; broken pipes, leaking taps, closed schools.

points.label: Corruption
points.text: Officials may steal funds meant for public facilities.

points.label: Access
points.text: Rural areas are harder to reach; remote villages often lack basic services.

example.problem: A public water pipe is broken for months. Why?
example.solution: Lack of funding, corruption, or poor maintenance. Officials must prioritize repairs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Providing public facilities is hard because money is limited and demands are huge.

image.alt: Challenges in Providing Public Facilities — Public Facilities

slides.title: Public Facilities in Rural vs. Urban Areas

points.label: Urban
points.text: Cities have more hospitals, schools, buses, and water supply—but are often overcrowded.

points.label: Rural
points.text: Villages often lack hospitals, good schools, paved roads, and reliable water.

points.label: Gap
points.text: Rural people travel hours for medical care or send children far for education.

points.label: Inequality
points.text: Poor rural areas have worse services than wealthy urban neighborhoods.

example.problem: Priya's village has no hospital within 20 km. A city hospital is 5 km away. Is this fair?
example.solution: No. This is rural-urban inequality. The government must invest in rural public facilities.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rural areas typically have fewer and worse public facilities than cities.

slides.title: Right to Public Facilities

points.label: Right to Water
points.text: Access to clean drinking water is recognized as a human right.

points.label: Right to Education
points.text: Article 21A guarantees free education for children 6–14.

points.label: Right to Health
points.text: Article 21 implies right to health through public services.

points.label: Accountability
points.text: If the government fails to provide, citizens can file complaints or petitions.

example.problem: Can Roshan's family demand public water supply from the government?
example.solution: Yes. The right to water is recognized, and they can demand the government provide it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Citizens have constitutional rights to basic public facilities.

image.alt: Right to Public Facilities — Public Facilities

slides.title: Real Example: Swachh Bharat Abhiyan (Clean India Campaign)
slides.storyContext: The government launched a nationwide campaign (2014) to build toilets and improve sanitation. Millions of families got public toilets, reducing open defecation and disease.

points.label: Scale
points.text: Over 100 million toilets built across India.

points.label: Impact
points.text: Better health, more girls attending school, improved dignity.

example.problem: How did Swachh Bharat improve public facilities for rural people?
example.solution: The government built public toilets and water systems, reducing disease and allowing girls to stay in school.

slides.inSimpleWords: Large government campaigns can rapidly improve public facilities and health.

image.alt: Real Example: Swachh Bharat Abhiyan (Clean India Campaign) — Public Facilities

slides.title: Check Your Understanding

points.label: Question
points.text: Your neighborhood's public park is damaged, with broken swings and dirty paths. Who is responsible to fix it? What should you do?

example.problem: What can you do if a public facility is not maintained?
example.solution: Contact the municipal office, file a complaint, organize community cleanup, or petition for repairs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Citizens can demand that governments maintain public facilities.

slides.title: Key Takeaways

points.text: Public facilities are government services available to all citizens.
Types include health, education, water, sanitation, transport, and recreation.
Public facilities ensure equality and meet basic needs of all people.
Rural areas often have fewer and worse public facilities than cities.
Citizens have rights to public facilities and can demand government action.

slides.inSimpleWords: Public facilities are essential for a fair, healthy, and developed society.

subject: Social Science
title: The Law That Saved Leela: Justice for All
hook: How do laws protect people from exploitation and abuse?

slides.title: Law and Social Justice
slides.inSimpleWords: How laws protect people's rights and ensure fair treatment for everyone.

slides.title: Leela's Rescue
slides.storyContext: Leela, age 10, is forced to work in a garment factory for 12 hours a day. She earns almost nothing. Inspector Maya raids the factory and finds Leela. A lawyer uses child labor laws to free her, hold the factory owner accountable, and get her into school.
slides.inSimpleWords: Laws protect vulnerable people like children from exploitation.

slides.title: What is Social Justice?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Social justice means fairness, equality, and protection for all, especially the vulnerable.

points.label: Pillars
points.text: Equal rights, equal opportunity, protection from harm, fair access to resources.

points.label: Vision
points.text: A society where no one is exploited, and all have dignity and chances to succeed.

example.problem: Is Leela being treated with social justice?
example.solution: No. She is exploited (forced child labor), denied education, and not treated fairly. Social justice demands her freedom.

slides.inSimpleWords: Social justice means a fair society where everyone is protected and has chances.

slides.title: Protection of Children (Child Rights)

points.label: Child Labor Act
points.text: Forbids children under 14 from working in mines, factories, or hazardous jobs.

points.label: Right to Education
points.text: Every child ages 6–14 has the right to free, compulsory education.

points.label: Right to Protection
points.text: Children have rights to safety, food, health, and freedom from abuse.

points.label: POCSO Act
points.text: Strict law against sexual abuse of children; conviction means jail and fine.

example.problem: Leela's factory owner keeps her working instead of letting her attend school. What laws protect her?
example.solution: Child Labor Act forbids her work; Right to Education Act ensures she attends school free. Both laws protect Leela.

slides.inSimpleWords: Laws protect children from labor, abuse, and deny them the right to education.

slides.title: Protection of Women (Women's Rights)

points.label: Dowry Prohibition Act
points.text: Taking or giving dowry is illegal; violators can be jailed or fined.

points.label: Domestic Violence Act
points.text: Protects women from abuse by husbands or family members; gives protection orders.

points.label: Equal Pay
points.text: Women must get equal wages as men for the same work.

points.label: Workplace Harassment
points.text: Law punishes sexual harassment at work; employers must have complaint cells.

example.problem: Leela's mother is beaten by her husband. What law protects her?
example.solution: The Domestic Violence Act. She can file a case, get a protection order, and the abuser can be punished.

slides.inSimpleWords: Laws protect women from dowry, violence, and discrimination.

slides.title: Protection of Workers (Labor Rights)

points.label: Minimum Wage
points.text: Employers must pay workers at least the legal minimum; cannot pay less.

points.label: Work Hours
points.text: Standard: 8 hours per day, 48 per week. Overtime must be paid extra.

points.label: Safe Workplace
points.text: Employers must provide safe conditions; injured workers get compensation.

points.label: Unions
points.text: Workers can form unions to bargain for better pay and conditions.

example.problem: A factory pays workers less than minimum wage and makes them work 14 hours. Is this legal?
example.solution: No. Labor laws set a minimum wage and maximum hours. The factory violates laws and can be sued.

slides.inSimpleWords: Labor laws ensure workers get fair pay, safe work, and reasonable hours.

slides.title: Protection Against Discrimination

points.label: Caste Act (SCST Act)
points.text: Punishes violence or discrimination against Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

points.label: Equal Opportunity
points.text: Jobs, education, and services cannot discriminate based on caste, religion, or gender.

points.label: Hate Speech
points.text: Speech inciting violence against a group is illegal.

points.label: Remedy
points.text: Victims can sue and get compensation if discriminated against.

example.problem: A hotel refuses to serve Leela because her family is Dalit. Is this legal?
example.solution: No. This is discrimination based on caste, which violates the SCST Act. Leela can file a case.

slides.inSimpleWords: Laws forbid discrimination based on caste, religion, or gender.

slides.title: Right to Information and Transparency

points.label: RTI Act
points.text: Any citizen can ask the government for information on its decisions.

points.label: Accountability
points.text: When governments must explain actions, they are less likely to be corrupt.

points.label: Example
points.text: Ask: "How much money did you spend on our public school?" The government must answer.

points.label: Whistle-blower
points.text: Workers who report corruption are protected by law.

example.problem: How can a community check if money for public schools is being stolen?
example.solution: File an RTI request asking the government to disclose spending. Transparency reduces corruption.

slides.inSimpleWords: RTI lets citizens demand transparency and expose government corruption.

slides.title: Real Example: Bhopal Gas Tragedy Justice
slides.storyContext: In 1984, a chemical plant leaked toxic gas, killing 2,000 people and injuring thousands. Survivors fought in courts for decades and won compensation.

points.label: Struggle
points.text: Took 16 years to get justice; company paid compensation to victims.

points.label: Lesson
points.text: Industries must follow safety laws or face punishment; victims have a right to justice.

example.problem: How did the Bhopal victims get justice?
example.solution: They filed cases using laws on corporate liability and right to life. Courts made the company pay compensation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Even after long struggles, laws help victims get justice and compensation.

slides.title: Check Your Understanding

points.label: Question
points.text: A factory owner fires a woman worker because she got pregnant. Is this legal? What laws protect her?

example.problem: Can a boss fire a woman for getting pregnant?
example.solution: No. Labor laws protect pregnant women. The company must give leave and cannot fire her. She can sue for damages.

slides.inSimpleWords: Laws protect workers from unfair firing.

slides.title: Key Takeaways

points.text: Social justice means fairness, equality, and protection for all, especially the vulnerable.
Laws protect children from labor and abuse; guarantee free education.
Laws protect women from dowry, violence, and discrimination.
Labor laws ensure workers get fair wages, safe conditions, and reasonable hours.
RTI and whistle-blower laws fight corruption and ensure transparency.

slides.inSimpleWords: Laws protect society's most vulnerable people and create a more just society.

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's Secret Garden Grid
hook: Priya is designing a square garden in Mumbai to plant herbs. Her friend Arjun wonders why squaring and cubing numbers matters for real life—until a giant terracotta cube planter arrives.

slides.title: Garden Grid Mystery
slides.storyContext: Priya sketches her dream herb garden: a perfect square plot in her Mumbai balcony. 'If each side is 8 meters, how many square meters of soil do I need?' Arjun laughs: 'Just count the tiles!' But there are too many. Priya shows him the shortcut: 8 × 8 = 64 square meters.
slides.inSimpleWords: A square number is a number times itself.

image.alt: Garden Grid Mystery — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Perfect Squares Defined

points.label: Definition
points.text: A perfect square is the product of a number multiplied by itself: n² = n × n

points.label: Visual
points.text: 3² forms a 3×3 grid = 9 unit squares (think chessboard tiles)

slides.inSimpleWords: Perfect squares are numbers that form grids.

image.alt: Perfect Squares Defined — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Example 1: Garden Area

example.problem: Priya's square garden has each side 6 meters. What is the total area?
example.solution: Area = side × side = 6 × 6 = 36 square meters. So 6² = 36.

slides.inSimpleWords: 6 squared equals 36 square meters.

image.alt: Example 1: Garden Area — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: The Giant Cube Planter
slides.storyContext: A massive terracotta cube arrives at Priya's building. Arjun opens the manual: 'This cube holds exactly 3 cubic meters of soil. How many unit cubes fit inside?' Priya thinks: 'If each edge is 2 meters... 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cubes!'
slides.inSimpleWords: A cube number is multiplying a number three times.

image.alt: The Giant Cube Planter — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Perfect Cubes Defined

points.label: Definition
points.text: A perfect cube is a number multiplied by itself three times: n³ = n × n × n

points.label: Volume Context
points.text: 3³ = 27 means a 3×3×3 cube holds 27 unit cubes (like sugar cubes stacked)

slides.inSimpleWords: Perfect cubes are numbers that form 3D blocks.

image.alt: Perfect Cubes Defined — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Example 2: Terracotta Planter

example.problem: A cubic planter has edges of 4 meters. What volume of soil fits inside?
example.solution: Volume = length × width × height = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cubic meters. So 4³ = 64.

slides.inSimpleWords: 4 cubed equals 64 cubic meters volume.

image.alt: Example 2: Terracotta Planter — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Squares and Cubes

points.text: Perfect squares (n²) are used for area of square plots.
Perfect cubes (n³) are used for volume of cubic containers.
Priya designs gardens, Arjun builds—both use math daily in Mumbai.

slides.inSimpleWords: Squares and cubes help measure space and volume.

image.alt: Squares and Cubes — A Square and A Cube
